To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

lay people's perspectives about the best ways to receive genomic secondary findings are influenced by the severity, familiarity, and lay illness representations (e.g. controllability, stigma) of the disease in question.

the perceived threat of a secondary finding (SF) is dependent on the severity of the disease, and that lay people may have very different illness representations and attitudes towards different diseases.
lay people react to hypothetical secondary findings in different ways, depending on perceived disease severity, familiarity of disease, and lay illness representations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ethical, clinical, and social implications of reporting back SFs to patients and research participants.
how lay people react when presented with hypothetical genomic secondary findings.
the ethical, social, and legal issues of genetic testing, specifically the reporting of secondary findings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lay perspectives are complex, and that the best way to report SFs depends on the disease and individual's illness representations.
the lay public would like more information about SFs, and that they would like this information to be presented in a sensitive manner, taking into account individual differences.

lay people's perspectives on SFs vary depending on the disease, and that SFs are perceived as more threatening for cancer than cardiovascular disorders, and less threatening than psychiatric or neurological disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the public is willing to accept genomic secondary findings, provided that the findings have clinical validity and utility and are presented in a clear and comprehensible way.
the lay people we interviewed would be more open to receiving genomic SFs for diseases that they perceived as severe, but for which there was a clear treatment available.
SF reporting should be tailored to individuals' illness perceptions, and that this may require a more individualized approach to SF reporting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SFs are not a single entity, but rather a heterogeneous collection of different disease types, each with its own characteristics and implications.
the reporting of SFs is not a one-size-fits-all endeavor and that the context and content of SF reporting may need to be adapted to different disease types.
SF reporting needs to consider the context of the SF and the recipient.
